notes_sections.title: Exam Domain Mapping
notes_sections.body:
| Domain | Relevance | Covered Ideas |
|---|---|---|
| D1: Agents and Workflows | None | This module does not teach workflow-vs-agent selection, manager/subagent hierarchies, the Agent SDK, custom loops, hooks, or context-window management. The "agent" in the code samples is a black box; the module never discusses its internals. |
| D2: Applications and Integration | High | Core module content: the systems lifecycle (requirements -> design -> build -> test -> deploy -> operate -> iterate), functional vs. infrastructure requirements, deployment-platform selection (first-party API, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock, Vertex AI, third-party platforms), configuration/version pinning of model IDs, and packaging a build as a configurable asset. |
| D3: Claude Code | Low | Claude Code is referenced only as one component in a multi-component workflow ("a Claude Code task fetches a customer page") and as a source of untrusted fetched content at a trust boundary. No coverage of Rules, Skills, Commands, Agent Memory, slash commands, or CLAUDE.md hierarchy. |
| D4: Eval, Testing, and Debugging | Low | Evals appear as the deployment gate (bundle the eval suite with an accelerator, run it against a pinned baseline before promoting a new model version) and as part of contribution readiness (a test proves the contribution works). No coverage of error-type identification, trace analysis, or isolating integration vs. model-output failures. |
| D5: Model Selection and Optimization | Medium | Model ID pinning vs. moving aliases, the mechanics of alias resolution changing behavior silently, per-platform model ID formats (Bedrock ARN vs. Bedrock Messages API `anthropic.` prefix vs. Vertex vs. first-party), and per-token cost as one input to total cost of ownership. Does not cover tokens/context windows, sampling, thinking modes, or shot-prompting. |
| D6: Prompt and Context Engineering | None | Not covered in this module. Prompt versioning is mentioned only in passing ("version the prompt and the asset alongside the code"), with no treatment of drift prevention, few-shot technique, or structured-output validation. |
| D7: Security and Safety | Medium | Trust boundaries as the organizing concept of the final teaching screen: treating fetched/untrusted content as data rather than instructions, least privilege scoped per component, the idea that a multi-component app is only as contained as its most privileged seam, and audit logging as part of what a regulated review requires. Builds directly on injection/access-control concepts from an earlier module but does not re-teach them. |
| D8: Tools and MCPs | Medium | MCP appears as one node in the multi-component integration map (an MCP server reaching a customer system on the app's behalf, scoped to least privilege, with access logged) and as a contribution channel (open-source MCP servers "each live in their own repository with their own contribution conventions"). No coverage of MCP resources/prompts, schema design, or built-in vs. custom vs. Skill vs. MCP tradeoffs. |

notes_sections.title: Key Concepts
notes_sections.body:
| Concept | Study Notes |
|---|---|
| Accelerator | A solution packaged so a future engagement configures a working asset instead of rebuilding from a blank repository. Built by separating customer-specific values from the reusable core and exposing the customer-specific parts as parameters with documented defaults. |
| Three accelerator asset types | Agent Template (system prompt, tool schemas, loop structure -> parameterize domain values), MCP Server Package (tools, inputs, scope -> document each tool input, let the installing team set scope), Eval Suite (dataset + rubric -> ship together so a new team can confirm the asset still works, and reuse the same suite as the deployment gate). |
| Packaging checklist (parameterize / document / bundle for audit) | For every asset type, decide: what to parameterize (values that change per customer: prompts, paths, scopes, credentials by reference, thresholds), what to document (environment assumptions, expected inputs, handled failure modes, the eval that defines "working"), and what to bundle for audit (data touched, identity acted under, log of what the asset did). |
| Hardcoding vs. parameterizing | Hardcoding customer-specific values (repo path, model name, thresholds, prompt fragments) ships faster under deadline but leaves nothing for the next team to configure; they must read the whole file to find load-bearing values, and without documentation or a bundled eval they end up rewriting from scratch. |
| Documentation covers what code cannot show | Code describes behavior; documentation covers the assumptions the asset makes about its environment, the inputs it expects, the failure modes it already handles, and the eval that defines whether it still works. Without it, the next team treats the asset as a black box. |
| Audit log as part of the package | A regulated customer's reviewer asks what data the asset touches, what identity it acts under, and what log it leaves. An accelerator without these passes a demo but stalls at the first security review. |
| Contributing back | Moving an asset from private (internal) reuse to shared infrastructure through a documented channel, so a team that never spoke to you can install it and get the same working setup. An asset already packaged for internal reuse (parameters, documented assumptions, bundled eval) is most of the way to what a maintainer needs. |
| Matching contribution to channel | The Claude Cookbook (GitHub repo of focused, self-contained reference implementations) is for a single- or multi-pattern example demonstrated end to end -- not a full multi-component application. Open-source MCP servers and tools each have their own repository and contribution conventions. A full application sent to the Cookbook stalls because reviewers are set up to review one focused pattern. |
| The four things that make a contribution verifiable | (1) The code does one thing -- a sprawling contribution forces the reviewer to reconstruct intent. (2) An example shows it running -- a reviewer should not have to build a harness. (3) A test proves it works -- lets the maintainer verify without reproducing your reasoning. (4) A short statement names the assumptions -- otherwise the first failure becomes the maintainer's problem. |
| Rights and attribution gate | Licensing and attribution are checked before technical review, because they decide whether a contribution can be accepted at all. Code carried in from a customer engagement may have constraints on where it can go. Confirm the right to contribute it and attribute anything built on. Skipping this turns the contribution into a legal problem later. If a licensing constraint cannot be cleared, escalate to the owner instead of contributing. |
| Functional requirement | Names what the system must do, stated with enough detail to check (e.g., "classify each ticket into one of four queues; draft a reply citing the relevant policy; never auto-send without human approval"). A vague business goal ("help support agents answer faster") is not yet a requirement. |
| Infrastructure requirement | Non-functional constraints the deployment must satisfy, derived by asking questions the business problem implies: Latency (how fast, measured where the user is), Scale (how many requests, at what peak), Residency (where must data be processed, under which regulation), Identity (who acts, under what credentials, what must be auditable). These four most often decide the deployment platform. |
| Documented requirements record | A short record covering functional behaviors, infrastructure constraints, and the regulation each constraint comes from, so a platform choice can be defended as following from requirements rather than from familiarity. Feeds directly into the deployment decision. |
| Systems lifecycle for a Claude application | Requirements (capture functional/infrastructure needs) -> Design (choose platform, model, trust boundaries) -> Build (write agent, tools, prompts) -> Test (evals, unit, integration, end-to-end) -> Deploy (pin version, gate promotion on eval) -> Operate (instrument cost, latency, errors; enforce guardrails) -> Iterate (feed production findings back into requirements). |
| Gates between lifecycle phases | A gate is a decision to move from one phase to the next, and it is where a regulated engagement keeps control: e.g., don't move design -> build until the platform satisfies the residency requirement; don't move deploy -> full production until the new version clears the eval against the pinned baseline. A one-off experiment may collapse phases; a regulated deployment cannot. |
| Deployment platform options | First-party Claude API (Anthropic's own environment, typically gets new features first, no binding cloud/residency constraint). Claude Platform on AWS (accessed via customer's AWS account, Anthropic's own model IDs/lifecycle, but inference is Anthropic-operated outside the AWS boundary). Claude in Amazon Bedrock (Messages API at `/anthropic/v1/messages`, broad feature parity -- confirm feature-specific gaps -- data stays inside the customer's AWS boundary). Claude on Amazon Bedrock (legacy) (InvokeModel/Converse APIs, ARN-versioned model identifiers). Google Vertex AI (Google Cloud identity/IAM, regional or global endpoints). Third-party platforms, e.g., Microsoft Foundry (embeds Claude inside a product the customer already uses; two hosting forms -- Hosted on Azure for a specific model subset with inference end-to-end on Azure, and Hosted on Anthropic for the rest, with inference on Anthropic infrastructure; residency depends on hosting form per model). |
| Customer's existing cloud drives the platform choice | The deployment-platform decision is rarely about technical merit alone; it is usually shaped by where the customer already has cloud infrastructure, identity management, and compliance agreements in place. |
| Identity and data residency are platform-determined | Identity and data location are answered by the platform, not your code. Bedrock uses AWS identity and keeps data inside the customer's AWS boundary; Vertex uses Google Cloud identity and boundary. Both offer regional routing when residency is a constraint. |
| Model alias vs. pinned model ID | An alias (e.g., "claude-haiku-4-5" pre-4.6, or names like "Opus"/"Sonnet") is convenient but evolves over time and may resolve to different versions across platforms -- an upstream change becomes a silent production change. A pinned full model ID (e.g., "claude-haiku-4-5-20251001" pre-4.6) resolves to a fixed snapshot. For Claude 4.6 and later, the model ID alone pins to a specific snapshot; for earlier models, the ID plus a date suffix is required. Always verify the current convention at platform.claude.com at build time. |
| Versioning discipline | Pin the specific model version (not the alias), version the prompt and the asset alongside the code, and keep the prior version available so a regression is a rollback rather than a hotfix. |
| Promotion gated by eval | Send a new model version to a portion of traffic, compare against the pinned baseline using the bundled eval suite, and promote or roll back based on the result. This is the eval acting as the deployment gate, not just a one-time test. |
| Per-platform versioning mechanics | First-party API and Claude Platform on AWS: pin the full model ID (same format), keep the prior snapshot; Anthropic's deprecation schedule applies. Claude in Amazon Bedrock: pin the full model ID with the `anthropic.` prefix; partner retirement dates differ from Anthropic's schedule. Claude on Amazon Bedrock (legacy): pin via ARN-versioned identifiers. Vertex AI: pin the full model ID before rollout using Vertex's format; partner retirement dates differ. Third-party platforms: pin per that platform's own versioning controls. |
| Comparing platforms on latency | Measure from the customer's actual region against their actual payload -- a laptop measurement hides the round-trip penalty. A platform in the customer's region shortens round-trip time; the first-party API is typically advantaged on earliest feature access. Within Bedrock, the global-vs-regional endpoint choice is also the primary residency control and can affect cost. |
| Comparing platforms on compliance | Often the dimension that ends the debate: a customer already certified on one cloud is unlikely to re-certify on another. Data residency = a rule that data must be processed in a specific country/region. The first-party API may not offer EU data residency (verify current coverage); EU-only residency typically requires Bedrock or Vertex AI. On Microsoft Foundry, hosting is per-model: Azure-hosted models run inference end-to-end on Azure, Anthropic-hosted Foundry models do not satisfy EU regional residency. For a regulated customer this is treated as pass/fail, not a tradeoff, and should be raised during scoping, not discovered at contract review. |
| Comparing platforms on cost | Per-token rates are broadly aligned across platforms; total cost moves on egress, platform fees, and integration effort. A lower token price can cost more once transfer and integration are counted. Instrument cost per call for each candidate platform. |
| Multi-component application | Coordinates more than one Claude capability into a single workflow (e.g., an API request triggers a Claude Code task, which reaches a customer system through an MCP server). Each component contributes a capability the others lack; every connection between them creates a place where identity, secrets, and untrusted input can cross. Map which component does what before connecting anything. |
| Trust boundary | The point where data or instructions move from one deployment environment to another -- exactly where injection and access controls apply. Content fetched by a Claude Code task is untrusted the moment it reaches the next component; the receiving component must treat it as data, not instructions. A component being trusted in isolation does not make the seam leaving it trustworthy -- trust does not carry over across a seam; each seam needs its own explicit control. |
| Least privilege across a multi-component app | Each component operates under an identity scoped to only the access its task needs. The application is only as contained as its most privileged seam -- one over-scoped component becomes the weak point even if every other component is properly scoped. |
| Multi-component integration map | First-party API: orchestrates the workflow, holds the entry point; boundary = the request entering from outside; control = input validation + the identity the call runs under. Claude Code task: runs agentic work, may fetch external content; boundary = the fetched content, untrusted downstream; control = treat fetched content as data at the next seam. MCP server: reaches a customer system to read or act; boundary = the system access held on the app's behalf; control = scope to least privilege and log the access. |
| Regulated review requires scoping the whole application | A regulated review requires justifying audit logging, data-residency decisions, and permission controls across the full application, not just one component. For regulated deployments, Bedrock and Vertex AI typically satisfy regional residency constraints. Confirm ZDR (zero data retention) and HIPAA BAA eligibility per component against the Anthropic Trust Center and platform.claude.com before scoping. |
| "Escalate, don't ship around it" pattern | Recurs three times in this module as the fallback when a normal fix isn't available: don't contribute code with an unclearable licensing constraint (escalate to the owner); use full lifecycle gating for a regulated deployment even under deadline pressure; when a trust-boundary seam cannot be secured, escalate to a human owner rather than shipping it. |

notes_sections.title: Decision Rules
notes_sections.body:
- If a build will be reused by another engagement, package it while fresh: separate customer-specific values into parameters, document assumptions, and bundle the eval and audit log. If it is a true one-off no one will reuse, skip packaging and ship.
- If a value differs per customer (prompt fragment, path, model name, threshold, scope, credential), it belongs in a parameter with a documented default, not hardcoded in the loop.
- If you are contributing a full multi-component application, do not send it to the Cookbook; strip it to a single focused pattern first, or route the specific piece (tool/server/fix) to its own repository.
- If a contribution lacks a runnable example, a test, or a stated set of assumptions, add them before opening it -- an unverifiable contribution sits at the back of the review queue regardless of code quality.
- If code was carried in from a customer engagement, confirm the right to contribute it and attribute prior work before any technical review; if the licensing constraint can't be cleared, escalate to the owner instead of contributing.
- If a requirement can be checked ("classify into one of four queues"), it is functional; if it constrains where/how fast/under what identity the system runs, it is infrastructure -- capture both before choosing a platform.
- If the customer already holds a compliance certification or cloud relationship, match the platform to it rather than to team familiarity, to avoid a residency review from scratch.
- If a regulated customer has a residency or compliance requirement, treat it as pass/fail and surface it during scoping, before design work is complete -- not at the go/no-go review.
- If shipping to production, pin the full model ID (not a moving alias) and keep the prior pinned version available for rollback.
- If promoting a new model version, gate the promotion on the bundled eval suite against the pinned baseline before sending full traffic to it.
- If measuring latency, compliance, or cost for a platform decision, measure from the customer's actual region/workload/certification -- not from your own laptop or team's default assumptions.
- If two or more Claude-powered components are wired together, mark every seam where data crosses as a trust boundary and add an explicit control there, even if each component passed its own tests in isolation.
- If a Claude Code task or any component fetches external/customer content, treat that content as data at the next seam, never as instructions to the next component.
- If a component needs system access (e.g., an MCP server reaching a customer system), scope its identity to least privilege and log what it does -- the whole app is only as contained as its most privileged seam.
- If a trust-boundary seam cannot be secured with an available control, do not ship around it -- escalate to a human owner.

notes_sections.title: Anti-Patterns
notes_sections.body:
- Hardcoding customer-specific values (repo path, model name, thresholds, prompt fragments) into a template and labeling it "reusable" without parameterizing, documenting, or bundling an eval.
- Shipping loose scripts instead of a template -- they run, but each customer-specific value is buried in a different file and diverges across copies instead of being configured in one asset.
- Sending a full multi-component application to the Cookbook instead of a focused, stripped-down example -- reviewers are set up for one pattern, not a whole app.
- Opening a contribution that is "the exact code that solved your problem" with no example, no test, and no stated assumptions -- it works for the author but the maintainer has nothing to verify it with.
- Skipping the rights/attribution check on engagement-derived code and treating licensing as a later cleanup step rather than a gate before technical review.
- Writing only a vague business goal ("be fast and accurate") and treating it as a requirement instead of deriving checkable functional and infrastructure requirements.
- Collapsing lifecycle gates under deadline pressure on a regulated engagement (e.g., moving to build before the platform's residency fit is confirmed, or promoting to full production without clearing the eval gate).
- Deploying against a moving model alias in production because it's the convenient default, with no prior pinned version retained for rollback.
- Choosing a deployment platform on team familiarity/ease of migration without checking the customer's residency or compliance requirements first.
- Measuring latency from a developer's laptop instead of from the customer's actual region and payload.
- Comparing platforms on token price alone while ignoring egress, platform fees, and integration effort, which are what actually move total cost.
- Wiring verified, individually-tested components together and assuming the seam between them is automatically trustworthy.
- Passing content fetched by one component (e.g., a Claude Code task) directly into the next component's call as if it were trusted instructions rather than untrusted data.
- Granting one component in a multi-component app broader access than its task requires, on the assumption that the other components are properly scoped so it "balances out."

notes_sections.title: Scenario Traps
notes_sections.body:
- Trap: "The template runs, so it's already an accelerator." Better: a template that runs has not been packaged for reuse -- packaging requires parameters, documented assumptions, and a bundled eval; those are different finishing states.
- Trap: "My PR works for me, so it's ready to submit as-is." Better: a maintainer accepts what they can verify -- add a runnable example, a test, and a short assumptions statement before opening it, or it stalls at the back of the queue.
- Trap: "This is useful, so it belongs in the Cookbook exactly as built, whole application and all." Better: match the contribution to the channel built for its shape; a full application overwhelms a review process built for one focused pattern -- strip it down or route pieces to their own repos.
- Trap: "The platform I know best is the fastest to build on, so it's the right choice." Better: ease of build answers whether the team can ship quickly, not whether the deployment will pass the customer's residency/compliance review -- check compliance constraints during scoping, before committing to a platform.
- Trap: "I measured latency and it looked fine (from my laptop)." Better: latency must be measured from the customer's actual region against their actual payload; a local measurement hides the real round-trip penalty.
- Trap: "Using an alias like 'opus' or 'claude-haiku-4-5' keeps me on the latest model for free." Better: an alias is a moving target that can change output shape without an app-code change; pin the full model ID and keep a prior version to roll back to.
- Trap: "All three components passed their own tests, so the wired-up app is safe." Better: a component trusted in isolation does not make the seam leaving it trustworthy -- every seam where data crosses between components needs its own explicit control.
- Trap: "The MCP server just reaches one customer system, so broad access is fine." Better: least privilege applies per component; the whole app is only as contained as its most privileged seam, so even one over-scoped component undermines the rest.
- Trap: "Compliance and platform choice are things to compare and weigh like latency or cost." Better: for a regulated customer, compliance/residency is typically pass/fail, not a tradeoff to balance against convenience.

notes_sections.title: Memorization Cues
notes_sections.body:
- Three accelerator types: Agent Template, MCP Server Package, Eval Suite -- each parameterize / document / bundle-for-audit.
- Contribution readiness = one thing it does + a runnable example + a test + a stated assumption, with rights/attribution cleared first.
- Lifecycle: Requirements -> Design -> Build -> Test -> Deploy -> Operate -> Iterate, with a gate between each phase.
- Requirements split: functional = what it must do (checkable behavior); infrastructure = latency, scale, residency, identity.
- Platform picks itself from the customer's existing cloud/compliance posture, not from team familiarity.
- Alias moves, pinned ID holds still: pin the full model ID, keep the prior version, gate promotion on the eval.
- Compare platforms on three things: latency (measured from the customer's region), compliance (pass/fail for regulated customers), cost (total per call, not token price alone).
- Trust boundary = wherever data crosses between deployment environments; treat fetched content as data, never as instructions.
- An app is only as contained as its most privileged seam -- least privilege must apply to every component, not just the risky-looking one.
- When a seam or a licensing constraint can't be resolved, escalate to a human owner rather than shipping around it.

notes_sections.title: Source References
notes_sections.body:
- Module Introduction: framing the module as "the point where code starts working is where this module's work begins" -- packaging, contributing, deploying/versioning, comparing platforms, and holding trust boundaries.
- Packaging for Reuse: accelerator definition, three asset types (template/server/eval), the packaging checklist, and the postmortem on a hardcoded template that could not be reused.
- Contributing Back: matching contribution to channel (Cookbook vs. tool/server repos), the four verifiability requirements, the rights/attribution gate, and the stalled-PR exchange between a developer and a maintainer.
- Requirements & Lifecycle: deriving functional and infrastructure requirements from a business problem, the seven-phase systems lifecycle for a Claude application, and gating between phases.
- Deployment & Versioning: the deployment-platform decision table (first-party API, Claude Platform on AWS, Bedrock, Bedrock legacy, Vertex AI, third-party/Microsoft Foundry), model alias vs. pinned ID, and the production incident caused by an unpinned alias.
- Comparing Platforms: measuring latency/compliance/cost per platform, and the postmortem on a platform chosen for familiarity that failed a customer's EU residency review.
- Trust Boundaries: mapping components before connecting them, the definition of a trust boundary, least privilege across the whole application, the multi-component integration map, and the "seam nobody marked as a boundary" pairing-session transcript.
- Cumulative Task: a single deployment snippet with three planted defects (one packaging, one deployment/versioning, one trust-boundary), diagnosed and then reassembled/corrected.
- Key Takeaways: five-point recap (package while fresh; maintainer accepts what they can verify; pin what ships; measure the dimension that decides placement; mark every seam as a boundary) plus the module's cited references (S1-S5: platform.claude.com deployment/versioning docs, Anthropic Cookbook/GitHub, Building with the Claude API course, Claude Code 101 In Action course).
- Glossary: Accelerator, Contribution readiness, Deployment platform, Model alias versus pinned ID, Trust boundary.

notes_sections.title: Gaps / Follow-Up
notes_sections.body:
- This module does not teach Agent SDK internals, custom agent loops, hooks, or context-window/memory management (D1) -- study those from the earlier "Production-Grade Prompting, Agents & Tool-use" module (M2) referenced in this course's own progress map.
- Does not cover Claude Code configuration mechanics (CLAUDE.md hierarchy, Rules, Skills, Commands, session management, slash commands) beyond naming a Claude Code task as one node in a multi-component workflow -- study the "Claude Code, MCP & Integration" module (M3).
- Does not cover eval/testing mechanics in depth (grading approaches, trace analysis, distinguishing integration failures from model-output failures) -- only that an eval suite is bundled with an asset and used as a deployment gate. See "Production Engineering, Evals, and Security" (M4) and the cited "Building with the Claude API" course (S4).
- Does not cover tokens, context windows, sampling, or thinking modes -- only model ID pinning/aliasing and per-platform ID formats. Confirm current model-ID/date-suffix conventions at platform.claude.com, since the module explicitly flags this as time-sensitive.
- Does not teach MCP server development mechanics (resources, tools, prompts, schema design) -- MCP appears only as a component in the trust-boundary map and as a contribution channel with its own repo conventions.
- Does not teach prompt-engineering technique (few-shot, output constraints, structured-output validation) -- prompt versioning is mentioned only as something to version alongside code and the asset.
- Injection defense and access-control mechanics are assumed prior knowledge from an earlier security module; this module applies them to trust boundaries but does not re-derive them. Cross-check against that module's notes for the underlying security concepts (prompt injection, guardrails, AAA/CIA).
- Verify at build/publish time: current model-ID pinning convention (date-suffix requirement pre- vs. post-4.6), Bedrock's features-not-supported list, Microsoft Foundry's current Azure-hosted vs. Anthropic-hosted model split, and each platform's current EU/regional residency and ZDR/HIPAA BAA coverage -- the module repeatedly flags these as time-sensitive and to be confirmed against platform.claude.com and the Anthropic Trust Center.

flashcards.question: What is an accelerator, in the sense this module uses the word?
flashcards.answer: A working solution packaged so that a future engagement configures a working asset rather than rebuilding from a blank repository -- customer-specific parts are separated out and exposed as parameters.
flashcards.example: A code-review agent built for one customer is turned into a template where the repo path, model ID, and thresholds are parameters instead of hardcoded values, so the next engagement just fills them in.

flashcards.question: What are the three categories most reusable work falls into, and what does each bundle?
flashcards.answer: Agent Template (system prompt, tool schemas, loop structure), MCP Server Package (exposed tools, their inputs, and the scope the installing team controls), and Eval Suite (the graded test set and judge rubric).
flashcards.example: A team packages a support-ticket agent as a template, wraps its ticketing integration as an MCP server, and ships the 20-ticket eval set alongside both so a new team can install and verify all three.

flashcards.question: For any accelerator asset, what three things does the packaging checklist require you to decide?
flashcards.answer: What to parameterize (values that change per customer), what to document (environment assumptions, expected inputs, handled failure modes, the defining eval), and what to bundle for audit (data touched, identity acted under, and the action log).
flashcards.example: For an MCP server package, the team parameterizes scopes and credential references, documents each tool's expected inputs, and bundles a log of every customer-system call the server made.

flashcards.question: In the module's packaging postmortem, why couldn't a second team reuse a shipped agent template?
flashcards.answer: Every customer-specific value (repo path, model name, thresholds, prompt fragments) was hardcoded into the loop with no parameters, no documentation of what was customer-specific, and no bundled eval to confirm it still worked -- so the second team had to rewrite it from scratch.
flashcards.example: A second engagement opens the "reusable" template, finds the review threshold buried inside a 200-line function, and gives up trying to configure it in favor of a full rewrite.

flashcards.question: What does documentation cover that the code itself cannot show a future builder?
flashcards.answer: The assumptions the asset makes about its environment, the inputs it expects, the failure modes it already handles, and the eval that defines whether it still works.
flashcards.example: A README note says "assumes the target repo has a `pyproject.toml` at the root; fails silently otherwise" -- a fact no amount of reading the agent loop would reveal quickly.

flashcards.question: Why does an accelerator need a bundled audit log, not just working code?
flashcards.answer: A regulated customer's reviewer asks what data the asset touches, what identity it acts under, and what log it leaves; an accelerator without that evidence passes a demo but stalls at the first security review.
flashcards.example: A bank's security reviewer rejects an otherwise-working summarization accelerator because it has no log showing which transcripts were read and under which service identity.

flashcards.question: What does "contributing back" mean in this module?
flashcards.answer: Moving an asset from private, internal reuse into shared infrastructure through a documented channel, so a team that never spoke to the author can install it and get the same working setup.
flashcards.example: A pattern for handling multi-turn customer-service conversations, built during one engagement, is generalized and submitted to the Claude Cookbook for anyone to use.

flashcards.question: Where does a full multi-component application belong versus a single focused tool?
flashcards.answer: A focused, self-contained pattern goes to the Claude Cookbook; a single tool or fix goes to its own tool/server repository with its own conventions; a full multi-component application is a mismatch for the Cookbook, which is built to review one focused pattern.
flashcards.example: A developer wants to share an entire customer-service app with UI and deployment scripts; it stalls in Cookbook review until only the reusable conversation-handling pattern is extracted and submitted on its own.

flashcards.question: What four things make a contribution something a maintainer can verify without reconstructing the author's intent?
flashcards.answer: The code does one thing, an example shows it running, a test proves it works, and a short statement names the assumptions.
flashcards.example: A PR wrapping a single API call includes a 10-line usage example, one test asserting the parsed response shape, and a note saying "assumes the API key is already set in the environment."

flashcards.question: In the module's stalled-PR exchange, why did a maintainer leave a working pull request unreviewed for three weeks?
flashcards.answer: The code worked for the author, but there was no test to run, no example proving the behavior, and nothing stating what it assumed about the environment -- so the maintainer had nothing to verify it with and it sat at the back of the queue.
flashcards.example: A developer says "the code works, I use it every day" and the maintainer replies that working for the author is not the same as being verifiable by a stranger.

flashcards.question: Why does licensing/attribution review happen before technical review of a contribution?
flashcards.answer: Licensing and attribution decide whether a contribution can be accepted at all; code carried in from a customer engagement may have constraints on where it can go, so confirming the right to contribute it is a gate the contribution must clear first.
flashcards.example: A one-line fix extracted from a customer engagement can't be merged until someone confirms the customer's contract doesn't restrict reuse of that code elsewhere.

flashcards.question: What should you do when engagement code carries a licensing constraint you cannot clear?
flashcards.answer: Do not contribute it -- escalate to the owner instead.
flashcards.example: A developer discovers the customer's MSA prohibits sharing derived code externally, so instead of quietly submitting a "cleaned up" version, they flag it to the engagement owner.

flashcards.question: What makes a statement a valid functional requirement rather than a vague business goal?
flashcards.answer: It names what the system must do with enough detail to check -- a checkable statement of behavior, not a general aspiration like "be fast and accurate."
flashcards.example: "Classify each ticket into one of four queues; draft a reply citing the relevant policy; never auto-send without human approval" is a functional requirement; "help support agents answer faster" is not.

flashcards.question: What four questions do you ask to derive infrastructure requirements from a business problem?
flashcards.answer: Latency (how fast, measured where the user is), Scale (how many requests, at what peak), Residency (where must data be processed, under which regulation), and Identity (who acts, under what credentials, what must be auditable).
flashcards.example: For an EU bank's call-summarization agent, the answers are: latency fast enough for support staff to act on, unspecified scale, EU-only residency, and a human identity that approves each summary before storage.

flashcards.question: For an EU bank's call-summarization agent, which is the functional requirement and which is the infrastructure requirement: "a human approves each summary before storage" vs. "transcript data must not leave the EU"?
flashcards.answer: "A human approves each summary before storage" is functional (checkable system behavior); "transcript data must not leave the EU" is an infrastructure/residency requirement (a non-functional deployment constraint).
flashcards.example: The functional requirement becomes an eval check ("was a summary ever stored without approval?"); the infrastructure requirement becomes a platform-selection constraint (choose Bedrock or Vertex with EU routing).

flashcards.question: What are the seven phases of the systems lifecycle as applied to a Claude application?
flashcards.answer: Requirements, Design, Build, Test, Deploy, Operate, Iterate.
flashcards.example: A team captures residency and latency needs (Requirements), picks Bedrock and a pinned model (Design), writes the agent (Build), runs evals (Test), ships behind a version gate (Deploy), tracks cost and errors in production (Operate), and feeds a recurring failure mode back into new requirements (Iterate).

flashcards.question: What is a "gate" in the systems lifecycle, and why does it matter for regulated engagements?
flashcards.answer: A gate is a decision point required to move from one phase to the next (e.g., not moving design to build until the platform satisfies residency, not promoting to production until the new version clears the eval against baseline); it is where a regulated engagement keeps control, and skipping it is what keeps deadline pressure from silently bypassing review.
flashcards.example: A team wants to start building against a platform before confirming it meets the customer's residency requirement; the gate blocks that move until Design confirms the platform choice.

flashcards.question: Which lifecycle phase does "pinning the full model ID and keeping the prior version" belong to, and which phase does "gating promotion on the eval result" belong to?
flashcards.answer: Pinning the model ID and retaining the prior version is a Deploy-phase activity; gating promotion on the eval result is also Deploy (the eval is the promotion gate at deployment).
flashcards.example: Both actions happen at the moment a new version is about to go live, not earlier during Build or Test.

flashcards.question: What is a "deployment platform" in this module's sense, and what usually determines which one is chosen?
flashcards.answer: The environment where the Claude workload runs (first-party API, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, or a third-party platform); the customer's existing cloud, identity management, and compliance agreements usually determine the choice more than technical merit.
flashcards.example: A customer already certified on AWS gets routed to Claude in Amazon Bedrock rather than the first-party API, to avoid a fresh compliance review.

flashcards.topic: First-Party API vs. Claude Platform on AWS
flashcards.question: What is the key difference between the first-party Claude API and Claude Platform on AWS?
flashcards.answer: The first-party API is Anthropic's own environment and typically gets new features first; Claude Platform on AWS is accessed through the customer's AWS account using Anthropic's own model IDs and lifecycle, but inference itself is Anthropic-operated, outside the AWS boundary.
flashcards.example: A customer wants to bill through their AWS account and use the same model IDs as the first-party API, but data still leaves the AWS boundary for inference -- so it does not satisfy an "inference must stay in AWS" residency rule.

flashcards.question: What are the two ways Claude is available through Amazon Bedrock, and how do they differ?
flashcards.answer: Claude in Amazon Bedrock uses the Messages API at `/anthropic/v1/messages` with broad feature parity to the first-party API (confirm feature-specific gaps); Claude on Amazon Bedrock (legacy) uses the InvokeModel/Converse APIs with ARN-versioned model identifiers.
flashcards.example: A team already using InvokeModel from an older integration keeps pinning via ARN-versioned identifiers rather than migrating immediately to the Messages API path.

flashcards.question: What are the two hosting forms Claude takes inside Microsoft Foundry, and why does the distinction matter for a regulated customer?
flashcards.answer: Hosted on Azure (a specific model subset, inference end-to-end on Azure infrastructure) and Hosted on Anthropic (all other Foundry Claude models, inference on Anthropic-operated infrastructure); residency assumptions depend on which hosting form the specific model uses, so it must be confirmed per model and deployment with Microsoft.
flashcards.example: A customer assumes all Foundry-hosted Claude models satisfy their EU residency rule, but an Anthropic-hosted Foundry model in their stack does not, because inference does not run entirely on Azure infrastructure.

flashcards.question: Does your application code determine where data is processed and under what identity, or does the platform?
flashcards.answer: The platform determines it, not your code -- Bedrock uses AWS identity and keeps data inside the customer's AWS boundary, Vertex uses Google Cloud identity and boundary, and both offer regional routing when residency is a constraint.
flashcards.example: Switching a workload from the first-party API to Bedrock changes its identity and residency posture even if not a single line of the agent's prompt or tool code changes.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between a model alias and a pinned full model ID, and why does it matter for production?
flashcards.answer: An alias (like "opus" or a pre-4.6 name without a date suffix) is convenient but evolves over time and can resolve to a different snapshot without warning; a pinned full model ID resolves to a fixed snapshot, so an upstream model change becomes a deliberate choice instead of a silent production change.
flashcards.example: `model = "claude-haiku-4-5"` can silently move to a new snapshot; `model = "claude-haiku-4-5-20251001"` stays fixed until the code is changed on purpose.

flashcards.question: How does model-ID pinning change starting with Claude 4.6?
flashcards.answer: For Claude 4.6 and later, the model ID alone pins to a specific snapshot; for earlier models, the ID plus a date suffix is required -- always verify the current convention at platform.claude.com at build time, since this is time-sensitive.
flashcards.example: A team building against Claude 4.6 no longer needs to append a date suffix to get a fixed snapshot, unlike their earlier Haiku 4.5 deployment.

flashcards.question: What three things does "pin what ships" require beyond just choosing a model ID?
flashcards.answer: Pin the specific model version (not the alias), version the prompt and the asset alongside the code, and keep the prior version available so a regression can be rolled back.
flashcards.example: A team ships v2 of both the model pin and the prompt template together, tagged in source control, with v1 still deployable if v2 regresses.

flashcards.question: In the module's "deployment that broke when the model alias moved" trace, what was the root cause and why couldn't the team roll back?
flashcards.answer: The application deployed against a moving alias; when the alias advanced to a new model version with no app change, the output shape changed and downstream parsing broke. Rollback failed because no pinned prior version had been retained.
flashcards.example: A parser expecting a `"summary"` key throws a KeyError overnight after an alias silently resolves to a new model version, and there's no earlier pinned snapshot to fall back to.

flashcards.question: How does an eval suite function differently at deployment time versus during initial development?
flashcards.answer: During development it is a one-time test that proves the asset works; at deployment it becomes a promotion gate -- a new version is sent to a portion of traffic, compared against the pinned baseline score, and promoted or rolled back based on the result.
flashcards.example: A new Sonnet version scores 2 points below the pinned baseline on the bundled eval, so the team holds it back from full traffic instead of promoting it.

flashcards.question: What three dimensions does this module say a deployment-platform choice must be measured on to survive a procurement/security review?
flashcards.answer: Latency, compliance, and cost.
flashcards.example: Before signing off, a security team wants to see measured round-trip latency from the customer's region, a compliance certification match, and a total-cost-per-call figure -- not just "we picked the platform we know."

flashcards.question: Why is a latency measurement taken from a developer's laptop unreliable for a platform decision?
flashcards.answer: The number is only accurate when measured from the customer's actual region against their actual payload; a laptop measurement hides the round-trip penalty that appears once the workload runs where the customer actually is.
flashcards.example: A platform tests at 180ms from a US developer's laptop but the customer's EU-based deployment sees much higher real-world latency once compliance-driven regional routing is added.

flashcards.question: How should a regulated customer's compliance/residency requirement be treated relative to latency and cost?
flashcards.answer: As pass-or-fail, not as a tradeoff to balance -- a regulated financial or healthcare customer will reject a platform that fails residency regardless of how well it performs on latency or cost.
flashcards.example: A platform with excellent latency and the lowest cost is still rejected outright because it cannot guarantee EU-only data processing for a regulated bank.

flashcards.question: Beyond per-token rate, what actually moves total deployment cost across platforms?
flashcards.answer: Data egress, platform fees, and integration effort -- per-token rates are broadly aligned across platforms, so a lower token price can still cost more once transfer and integration are factored in.
flashcards.example: Platform A has a slightly higher token price but no egress fees and minimal integration work, ending up cheaper overall than Platform B's lower token price plus heavy data-transfer charges.

flashcards.question: In the module's "platform picked on familiarity" postmortem, why was the integration rejected at security review despite passing functional tests?
flashcards.answer: The team chose the platform they knew best because migration was fast, but that platform did not satisfy the customer's data-residency requirement; a different, less-familiar platform with regional deployment options would have satisfied it. The compliance check happened too late, at the security review instead of during scoping.
flashcards.example: A reviewer asks "where is data processed?" at the go/no-go review, and the answer disqualifies a platform whose only advantage had been that the team already knew how to build on it.

flashcards.question: What is a multi-component application in this module's sense, and what risk does connecting components introduce?
flashcards.answer: An application coordinating more than one Claude capability into a single workflow (e.g., an API request triggers a Claude Code task, which reaches a customer system through an MCP server); every connection between components creates a place where identity, secrets, and untrusted input can cross.
flashcards.example: An API entry point calls a Claude Code task to fetch a webpage, then passes that content into an MCP-server-backed call against a customer database -- three components, at least two seams.

flashcards.question: What is a trust boundary, and where does it apply the injection/access-control principles from earlier security work?
flashcards.answer: The point where data or instructions move from one deployment environment to another; it is exactly where injection defenses and access controls apply -- content fetched at one component is untrusted the moment it reaches the next component and must be treated as data, not instructions.
flashcards.example: Content a Claude Code task fetched from a customer's public webpage is untrusted the instant it is handed to the next component in the pipeline, even though the Claude Code task itself ran correctly.

flashcards.question: If every component in a multi-component app passed its own tests individually, is the seam connecting them automatically trustworthy?
flashcards.answer: No -- a component being trusted in isolation does not make the seam leaving it trustworthy; each seam where data crosses needs its own explicit control, because trust does not carry over across a boundary.
flashcards.example: Dev A wires up three individually-tested components and assumes it's safe; Dev B points out that the fetched content flowing into the next call was never marked as untrusted data at that seam.

flashcards.question: In the module's "seam nobody marked as a boundary" transcript, what specifically went wrong?
flashcards.answer: A Claude Code task's fetched content was passed straight into the next component's call as part of the prompt, with no control treating it as untrusted data; if the fetched content carried instructions, the next component would run them, because the seam between the two trusted components was never marked as a boundary.
flashcards.example: `next_call(input=fetched)` runs fetched webpage content directly as part of the next prompt with no sanitization or "treat as data" wrapping.

flashcards.question: How does least privilege apply differently to a multi-component application than to a single component?
flashcards.answer: It applies to the application as a whole -- each component should get only the access its specific task needs, and the application is only as contained as its most privileged seam; one over-scoped component becomes the weak point even if every other component is properly scoped.
flashcards.example: If the orchestrating API component has full database write access "just in case," that access is the real risk even though the MCP server itself is tightly scoped to read-only.

flashcards.question: For the three components in this module's integration map (first-party API, Claude Code task, MCP server), what is each one's boundary and control?
flashcards.answer: First-party API: boundary is the incoming request; control is input validation plus the identity the call runs under. Claude Code task: boundary is the content it fetched, untrusted downstream; control is treating that content as data at the next seam. MCP server: boundary is the system access it holds on the app's behalf; control is scoping to least privilege and logging the access.
flashcards.example: An MCP server that reaches a customer's ticketing system is scoped to read-only ticket access and logs every call it makes, satisfying its column in the map.

flashcards.question: What must a regulated review justify across a multi-component Claude application?
flashcards.answer: Audit logging, data-residency decisions, and permission controls across the full application -- not just one component -- with ZDR and HIPAA BAA eligibility confirmed per component against the Anthropic Trust Center and platform.claude.com before scoping.
flashcards.example: A healthcare customer's review asks not just "is the MCP server scoped correctly" but "does every component in this pipeline, including the orchestrating API, satisfy our BAA and residency requirements."

flashcards.question: What should you do when a trust-boundary seam in a multi-component app cannot be secured with an available control?
flashcards.answer: Do not ship around it -- escalate to a human owner.
flashcards.example: A team can't find a reliable way to sanitize content fetched from an uncontrolled external source before it reaches the next component, so they flag the design to their security lead instead of shipping with an unmarked seam.

flashcards.question: The module's cumulative diagnostic task plants one defect in each of which three layers?
flashcards.answer: The packaging layer (a hardcoded customer-specific value where a parameter belongs), the deployment-and-versioning layer (an unpinned model alias instead of a full pinned model ID), and the multi-component boundary layer (fetched content passed into the next call untreated as untrusted data).
flashcards.example: The shipped snippet has `model="opus"` (unpinned alias, defect 2), a hardcoded `repo_path` (defect 1), and `next_call(input=fetched)` with no data-vs-instructions handling (defect 3) -- three separate fixes across three separate module topics.

flashcards.question: What single idea ties together packaging, contributing, deployment/versioning, platform comparison, and trust boundaries in this module?
flashcards.answer: The point where code starts working is where this module's work begins -- a working build is not yet reusable, verifiable, deployable-on-purpose, defensible to procurement/security, or safe across its own seams; each topic makes that gap concrete in a different area.
flashcards.example: A working demo agent still needs parameters and a bundled eval to be reused, a test and example to be contributed, a pinned model ID to be deployed safely, measured latency/compliance/cost to be defended, and marked seams to pass a multi-component security review.

practice_questions.scenario: A developer just finished a code-review agent for a customer engagement. It works well and the deadline is tomorrow. The team lead asks whether it should be packaged as a reusable accelerator before the engagement closes.
practice_questions.prompt: According to the module, what is the strongest reason to package it now rather than later?

choices.text: Packaging is required by the Claude Cookbook before any code can be contributed.
The knowledge of what is customer-specific is cheapest to capture while the build is fresh, and gets more expensive to reconstruct after the people who knew it have moved on.
A packaged accelerator automatically passes a security review, while an unpackaged one does not.
Packaging is only necessary if the code will be open-sourced externally.

practice_questions.explanation: The module's core argument for packaging while the build is fresh is that the knowledge of which values are customer-specific and which are load-bearing is most expensive to reconstruct later, once the person who made those decisions has moved on to other work.

distractors.A: Packaging for internal reuse and contributing to the Cookbook are related but separate motions; the Cookbook is not a prerequisite gate for packaging.
distractors.C: Packaging helps a security review (via the bundled audit log) but does not automatically pass one; a reviewer still checks the specifics.
distractors.D: The module frames packaging as valuable for any future engagement reuse, not only for external open-sourcing.

practice_questions.scenario: A team ships an agent template with the customer's repository path, model name, and review thresholds hardcoded directly into the function body. Months later, a second team tries to reuse it for a similar engagement and cannot configure it.
practice_questions.prompt: What is the most accurate diagnosis of what went wrong?

choices.text: The template should have used a newer model version.
The template ran successfully, so it was already reusable; the second team simply lacked the context to use it.
A template that runs is not the same as a template packaged for reuse -- the customer-specific values needed to be parameters, and the assumptions and eval needed to be documented and bundled.
The template needed to be rewritten in a different programming language for portability.

practice_questions.explanation: The module's postmortem makes this exact distinction: a working template and a reusable one are different finishing states. Hardcoded values with no documentation and no bundled eval leave the next team nothing to configure, forcing a rewrite.

distractors.A: Model choice is unrelated to the packaging defect described.
distractors.B: This is the trap the postmortem exists to correct -- running is not the same as reusable.
distractors.D: Language choice was never the issue; the issue was hardcoded values and missing documentation/eval.

practice_questions.scenario: A developer wants to share a small, focused utility function that wraps a single API call into a clean interface, built during a customer engagement. The code has no example, no test, and no note on what it assumes about its environment.
practice_questions.prompt: What should the developer do before opening this as a contribution?

choices.text: Submit it as-is, since a maintainer can read the function and infer its behavior.
Add a runnable example, a test that proves the behavior, and a short statement of assumptions, and confirm the right to contribute code that originated in an engagement.
Rewrite it as a full application with a UI so reviewers can see it in context.
Skip the Cookbook entirely and only distribute it privately within the team, since packaging for external contribution is optional.

practice_questions.explanation: A maintainer accepts what they can verify. The module names four requirements for a verifiable contribution -- focused code, a runnable example, a test, and stated assumptions -- and requires the rights/attribution check before technical review, especially for engagement-derived code.

distractors.A: This repeats the exact failure mode from the module's stalled-PR case; "the maintainer can figure it out" is what leaves a contribution at the back of the queue.
distractors.C: A full application with a UI is a mismatch for a focused utility contribution and would itself violate the "match contribution to channel" guidance.
distractors.D: The scenario asks what to do to make the contribution viable, not whether to contribute at all; nothing in the module makes external contribution optional once a team decides to pursue it.

practice_questions.scenario: A developer wants to contribute an entire customer-service application -- including its UI and deployment scripts -- to the Claude Cookbook, because it is a working, well-tested system.
practice_questions.prompt: What is the best assessment of this plan?

choices.text: It is correct, because the Cookbook is designed to hold complete, deployable applications.
It is a mismatch: the Cookbook is built to review one focused, self-contained pattern, not an entire application, so the submission should be reduced to the reusable pattern before contributing.
It is correct, provided the application includes a full test suite.
It should go through the same repository as any open-source MCP server contribution.

practice_questions.explanation: The module explicitly calls sending a full application to the Cookbook one of the most common reasons a contribution never gets reviewed, because the Cookbook's review process is built for a single focused pattern demonstrated end to end.

distractors.A: This is the opposite of what the module states about Cookbook scope.
distractors.C: A test suite does not resolve the channel mismatch -- the problem is scope, not verification quality.
distractors.D: MCP servers and tools have their own separate repositories with their own conventions; a full customer-service application is neither an MCP server nor a simple tool fix.

practice_questions.scenario: An EU-based regulated bank wants an agent that summarizes customer call transcripts, with each summary reviewed by a human before being stored, and all transcript data processed inside the EU.
practice_questions.prompt: Which of the following is the infrastructure requirement (as opposed to the functional requirement) in this scenario?

choices.text: The agent produces a summary that a human approves before it is stored.
Transcript data must be processed inside the EU.
The agent should be fast and accurate.
The agent uses a pre-approved prompt template.

practice_questions.explanation: Infrastructure requirements are non-functional deployment constraints derived from questions like residency ("where must data be processed, under which regulation"). Requiring EU-only processing is a residency constraint, which is an infrastructure requirement.

distractors.A: Human approval before storage describes checkable system behavior, making it a functional requirement, not an infrastructure one.
distractors.C: "Fast and accurate" is not a valid requirement of either kind -- it's a vague goal that lacks the detail needed to check or design against.
distractors.D: Using a pre-approved prompt template is closer to a functional/behavioral choice than an infrastructure constraint about where or under what identity the system runs.

practice_questions.scenario: A team deploys a production application against the alias `"opus"` because it's convenient and automatically stays on the recommended model. Months later, the alias silently advances to a new underlying version, the output shape changes, and a downstream parser breaks. The team tries to roll back but finds no prior pinned version was retained.
practice_questions.prompt: What is the root cause, and what should have been done differently?

choices.text: The root cause was a parser bug; the fix is to make the parser more defensive against any output shape.
The root cause was using an unpinned alias with no prior version retained; the fix is to pin the full model ID and keep the prior pinned version available for rollback.
The root cause was choosing Opus over Sonnet; the fix is to switch model tiers.
The root cause was not running the eval suite in development; the fix is to add more unit tests to the agent's tool functions.

practice_questions.explanation: This mirrors the module's alias-incident trace directly: the application never changed, but the alias did, and with no pinned prior version retained there was nothing to roll back to. The fix named in the module is pinning the full model ID, keeping the prior version, and gating promotion through the eval.

distractors.A: A more defensive parser might reduce symptoms but does not address the root cause of an untracked, unpinned production change.
distractors.C: The model tier (Opus vs. Sonnet) is unrelated to the alias-vs-pinned-ID problem described.
distractors.D: The module frames the eval as the deployment gate for promoting new versions, not primarily as a unit-testing exercise for tool functions; the described failure is specifically about the absence of pinning and rollback capability.

practice_questions.scenario: A team needs to choose a deployment platform for a customer who already runs entirely on AWS and holds an existing compliance certification there, and who also needs the ability to roll back a future model update.
practice_questions.prompt: Which combination best satisfies this scenario, per the module's guidance?

choices.text: First-party Claude API, using an Anthropic API key, with a moving alias for the model reference and no version retention.
Amazon Bedrock, using an AWS identity reference, with a pinned full model ID, retaining the prior pinned version for rollback.
Google Vertex AI, using an AWS identity reference, with a moving alias for the model reference.
First-party Claude API, using an AWS identity reference, with a pinned full model ID.

practice_questions.explanation: The customer's existing AWS presence and compliance posture point to Amazon Bedrock, which uses AWS identity and keeps data inside the customer's AWS boundary. Rollback capability requires a pinned full model ID (not a moving alias) plus retaining the prior pinned version.

distractors.A: The first-party API does not match an AWS-committed, already-certified customer, and a moving alias with no version retention makes rollback impossible -- the opposite of what the scenario needs.
distractors.C: Vertex AI uses Google Cloud identity, not AWS identity; mixing an AWS identity reference with Vertex is not how the module describes the platforms working, and a moving alias again defeats rollback.
distractors.D: The first-party API uses Anthropic identity and terms, not an AWS identity reference, so this combination misassigns the identity model to the platform.

practice_questions.scenario: A team measures the latency of a candidate deployment platform from a developer's laptop in the United States and gets a fast result. The customer's actual users and data are in the EU, and the customer also holds an existing compliance certification on a different cloud provider.
practice_questions.prompt: What is the strongest critique of this team's evaluation approach?

choices.text: The latency measurement should have been taken from the customer's actual region against their actual payload, and the compliance certification the customer already holds should weigh heavily on the platform choice.
Latency measurements are irrelevant to platform choice; only compliance matters.
The team should optimize the parser to reduce measured latency further.
The measurement is valid as long as the platform is technically capable of running in the EU.

practice_questions.explanation: The module is explicit that latency numbers are only accurate when measured from the customer's actual region against their actual payload, and that compliance often ends the debate because a customer already certified on one cloud is unlikely to re-certify on another.

distractors.B: The module treats latency, compliance, and cost as three dimensions to measure together, not as one dimension replacing the others.
distractors.C: Parser optimization does not address the fact that the measurement itself was taken from the wrong location, which is the actual defect here.
distractors.D: Technical capability to run in the EU says nothing about the measured latency from the customer's actual location, nor about whether the platform matches the customer's already-held compliance certification.

practice_questions.scenario: A multi-component application wires an API entry point to a Claude Code task that fetches a customer's public webpage, then passes that fetched content directly into the next component's call as part of its prompt. All three components individually passed their own unit tests before being connected.
practice_questions.prompt: What is the security gap in this design, and what should be done about it?

choices.text: There is no gap, because each component already passed its own tests before being wired together.

The fetched content is untrusted the moment it leaves the Claude Code task; the seam receiving it needs an explicit control treating that content as data, not as instructions, regardless of how well each component tested in isolation.
The gap is that the API entry point lacks a caching layer, which should be added to reduce redundant fetches.
The gap is that the MCP server was not used to fetch the content instead of the Claude Code task.

practice_questions.explanation: This matches the module's "seam nobody marked as a boundary" case directly: a component being trusted in isolation does not make the seam leaving it trustworthy. Fetched content is untrusted downstream and must be explicitly treated as data at the next seam, exactly as the security-module injection principles require.

distractors.A: This is precisely the mistaken reasoning the module's example dialogue calls out -- individual test passage says nothing about the untested seam between components.
distractors.C: Caching addresses performance, not the trust-boundary problem of unmarked, unvalidated content crossing into the next component as if it were instructions.
distractors.D: Which component fetches the content is not the issue; the issue is that whichever component fetches it, the receiving seam must treat that content as data.

practice_questions.scenario: A regulated healthcare customer's security review requires justifying audit logging, data-residency decisions, and permission controls across an entire multi-component application: a first-party API entry point, a Claude Code task, and an MCP server that reaches a patient-records system with full read/write access "to keep things simple."
practice_questions.prompt: Based on the module's guidance on least privilege, what is the most likely outcome of this review, and why?

choices.text: The review passes, because the MCP server is the only component that touches sensitive data, and its correctness is what matters.

The review likely fails on the MCP server's scope: the application is only as contained as its most privileged seam, so full read/write access where read-only would suffice becomes the weak point even if the other components are well-scoped.
The review passes as long as the first-party API entry point performs input validation, regardless of how the MCP server is scoped.
The review outcome depends only on which deployment platform was chosen, not on how individual components are scoped.

practice_questions.explanation: The module states directly that an application is only as contained as its most privileged seam -- a single component scoped too broadly becomes the weak point even when every other component is properly scoped. Full read/write access "to keep things simple" is exactly the over-scoping the least-privilege discipline is meant to prevent.

distractors.A: The module rejects this framing; least privilege applies to the whole application, and an over-scoped component undermines the rest regardless of its own "correctness."
distractors.C: Input validation at the entry point is one necessary control among several, but it does not compensate for an over-scoped MCP server elsewhere in the chain.
distractors.D: Platform choice (e.g., Bedrock vs. Vertex) affects residency and identity models, but component-level scoping is a separate discipline that a platform choice alone does not resolve.
